prompt:
Write 9 short claim log entries (one to three sentences each) by an auto insurance adjuster for a side impact at intersection claim, in time order. Injury: neck strain. The claimant is not represented by a lawyer. Start each entry on a new line with 'Entry 1:', 'Entry 2:' and so on. No names, dates or amounts. (Internal reference C-1222; do not mention it.) Work these facts into the text naturally, in your own words, without listing them:
- The reported injury matches the kind and force of the crash well.
- Treatment followed a usual course and tapered off as the patient improved.
- No earlier injury to the same body area is known.
- Witnesses, photos and the other driver all confirm the accident happened as described.
- The vehicle damage matches the described impact.
- The claimant told the same account in every conversation.
- The police and witnesses confirm the claimant was in the vehicle.
- No earlier damage to the vehicle is known.
- A neighbor thinks the car was damaged some weeks before the claimed date.
- The driver is named on the policy.
text:
Entry 1: The claimant reported a side impact at a controlled intersection, with the claimant's vehicle struck on the driver's side by another vehicle that entered from the cross street. The claimant said the claimant was in the vehicle and the driver is named on the policy.

Entry 2: Police attended the scene and confirmed the claimant was seated in the vehicle when it was struck. Two independent witnesses were located and both described the collision in the same sequence the claimant gave.

Entry 3: The other driver gave a statement that matches the claimant's account of the signal phase and the point of impact. Scene photographs show the damage pattern lining up with the reported direction of force.

Entry 4: The vehicle was inspected at the repair facility, and the damage to the driver's side panels, door and rear quarter is consistent with the impact described. No earlier damage to the vehicle is known from our records or from the repair history provided.

Entry 5: The claimant attended urgent care the same day with neck pain and stiffness, which the examining clinician recorded as a strain. The injury is a good fit for the kind and force of a side impact of this type, and no prior injury to the neck or upper back is known.

Entry 6: The claimant was contacted by phone and again in person, and the account of the accident has stayed the same each time, including the sequence of events and the position of the vehicles. The claimant is not represented by an attorney and has been responsive to requests for records.

Entry 7: A neighbor who was contacted during the investigation said they believed the vehicle showed body damage some weeks before the reported collision. The neighbor could not give a firm date or describe the damage, so this recollection is being noted and will be checked against the repair history and any available photographs.

Entry 8: Treatment followed a usual course, with physiotherapy sessions tapering as the claimant's range of motion and pain improved. The treating provider's notes show steady progress and a plan to discharge the claimant from active care once goals are met.

Entry 9: The neighbor's recollection was reviewed against the repair records and the photographs taken at the scene, and no record supports earlier damage. Based on the evidence gathered, the claim is progressing toward evaluation of the neck strain with the treatment and recovery timeline noted.
